stories.headline: Senate Republicans plan 54-day blitz to push Trump's agenda before Democrats seize power
stories.note: Senate Republicans are racing to lock in Trump's agenda while they still hold the gavel.
body: Senate Republicans, fresh off their leadership elections, have agreed to a year-end sprint to get as much done as possible before Democrats take control of the chamber next year.
Majority Leader John Thune, re-elected as GOP leader, said the plan means more days in session, longer hours and more votes. "We are going to finish this legislative session strong," Thune said.

A resolution adopted at Tuesday's closed-door meeting, obtained by Fox News Digital, commits the conference to use its 54 remaining days to confirm every approved judicial and executive nominee, pass core GOP priorities and try to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3. As of Tuesday there were 23 judicial nominees and nearly 100 executive nominees awaiting action.

Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson planned to present a reconciliation framework Wednesday, and Republicans are weighing one more attempt at a version of the SAVE America Act to fund state election-integrity efforts. Thune cautioned the bill likely needs to stay narrow to pass, and said it could also carry Pentagon money if Democrats use spending fights to choke off funding for the Iran war.

Other must-do items include the defense authorization bill, a bipartisan permitting package and keeping the government funded. Sen. Katie Britt said she hopes Democrats will still work with Republicans to clear those decks.
Why it matters: With the majority slipping away, Republicans are trying to lock in judges, nominees and priorities like election integrity while they still control the Senate floor.

stories.headline: House GOP leaders block Massie's Hegseth impeachment push
stories.note: House GOP leadership shut down the impeachment push against the War Secretary.
body: House Republican leaders stopped Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, winning a 211-204 vote Tuesday evening to send the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, which effectively killed it.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had forced the issue with a privileged resolution containing eight articles touching on the Iran war, strikes on suspected drug boats and Hegseth's actions against Sen. Mark Kelly. Every Democrat present backed moving ahead; every Republican except Massie voted to shelve it.

President Trump cheered the outcome on Truth Social, writing that the Democrats' attempt to impeach Hegseth "has miserably FAILED!" Hegseth had earlier called the effort a political spectacle driven by ego and resentment.

GOP leaders had worried that absences after last week's midterm losses could open the door to an actual impeachment vote, but Speaker Mike Johnson managed one more win on his way out. Even Hegseth critics like Reps. Don Bacon and Warren Davidson said they did not agree with Massie's articles.
Why it matters: Republicans held together under pressure and denied Democrats a high-profile vote against one of Trump's top Cabinet officials, at least for now.

stories.headline: Jim Jordan becomes new House GOP leader after closed-door vote, defeating Steve Scalise
stories.note: House Republicans pick a proven fighter to lead them into the next Congress.
body: House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio won a closed-door race Tuesday to become House Republicans' leader in the next Congress, defeating Majority Leader Steve Scalise 106 to 73, according to sources in the room.

Sources said loud, sustained applause could be heard in the hallway when the result became official. Majority Whip Tom Emmer also beat Rep. August Pfluger 103 to 76 for the No. 2 job of minority whip, and Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain survived a challenge.

The secret-ballot vote included current members and projected members-elect, and followed a historic midterm loss that led Speaker Mike Johnson to step aside from leadership. At a morning forum, both Jordan and Scalise pitched themselves as unifiers.
Allies praised Jordan as an effective outsider to leadership. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald said Jordan "understands what we're up against," calling his communication skills unrivaled in the House.
Why it matters: Jordan, one of Trump's most vocal defenders, will lead the GOP pushback as Democrats prepare a wave of investigations into the president's Cabinet, family and businesses.

stories.headline: Florida AG subpoenas DSA over potential illegal funding from Cuba and China
stories.note: Florida is putting the Democratic Socialists' money under the microscope.
body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office has issued an investigative subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America over whether the group took contributions from foreign sources of concern, including in Cuba and China.

The subpoena seeks records about recent DSA delegations to China and Cuba, where members met with Cuban government officials, to determine whether the group violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
"We will not allow foreign adversaries to influence Florida through the backdoor," Uthmeier said in a video statement. He did not detail specific criminal allegations or name any individuals.

The DSA has praised the Cuban regime and pushes to end the U.S. embargo. According to a State Department report cited in the article, DSA members met privately with Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel during a 2023 trip.
Why it matters: The probe comes just after DSA-backed candidates won races across the country, putting the left's rising socialist wing and its foreign ties under legal scrutiny.

stories.headline: Democrats accused of 'No Kings' hypocrisy over push to change voter-approved trans sports measures
stories.note: Democrats are under fire for trying to undo what voters approved on girls' sports.
body: Voters in Colorado and Washington state, both Democratic strongholds, approved limits on transgender athletes in girls' sports last week. Now Democratic leaders in both states are talking about changing the results, and Republicans are calling it hypocrisy.

In Colorado, Gov.-elect Philip Weiser suggested the Democratic legislature could make adjustments to the voter-approved measures, which also included tougher fentanyl penalties and a ban on gender-related surgeries for minors. Adams County Republicans dubbed him "King Phil I."

In Washington, Initiative 638 passed with about 56% support. Rep. Pramila Jayapal reportedly vowed to plan how to overturn it, and state Democratic Party chair Shasti Conrad signaled support for a court challenge, calling it unconstitutional.

Critics pointed out that both Weiser and Jayapal have backed the anti-Trump "No Kings" movement, with Colorado House Republicans saying Democrats should take their own advice. Under Washington's constitution, lawmakers need a two-thirds vote to amend an initiative in its first two years.
Why it matters: Even in a blue-wave year, voters in deep-blue states sided with the GOP position on girls' sports, and Democrats moving to undo those votes hands Republicans a powerful message.

stories.headline: Dead felons, dog and now a prisoner: Spanberger voting rights letters draw fresh scrutiny
stories.note: More embarrassing errors pile up for Virginia Democrat Spanberger's voting-rights mailers.
body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's voting-rights restoration program is under new scrutiny after a restoration letter was mailed in the name of a woman who is still in prison on a felony drug conviction.

It's the latest in a string of errors: earlier letters went to a Goochland County dog that died five years ago, to a sheriff's office addressed to "Betty No Last Name," and to families of deceased felons.

A resident with no known connection to the prisoner, Kayla Renae Vaughn, received the letter and contacted GOP Del. Tom Garrett. State records show Vaughn is serving her sentence at a Chesterfield County prison. House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore said restoring rights to someone still incarcerated would mark "a new level of carelessness."

Garrett noted that each letter claims the administration reviewed the individual case, which a past Virginia Supreme Court ruling requires. The new voter-approved amendment also excludes people still serving felony prison sentences. Spanberger and her secretary of the commonwealth did not respond to requests for comment.
Why it matters: The mistakes undercut a Democratic governor's signature election policy and bolster Republican warnings about sloppy voter-roll practices.

stories.headline: Top Dem cries 'weaponization' as comments warning young people not to join Trump admin land her in hot water
stories.note: A top Democrat's warning to young people backfires and lands her in trouble.
body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan is accusing President Trump of a coordinated weaponization campaign after he ordered the Justice Department to look into her October remarks warning young Republicans they could face "a ton of problems" if they join his administration.

Slotkin made the comments Oct. 13 at a University of Chicago event about how Democrats might use congressional power. She also reportedly advocated pursuing cases against people who enabled Trump. A student who publicized the remarks filed a Senate ethics complaint on Oct. 22.

In a Monday video, Slotkin said she only meant people breaking the law or misusing taxpayer money, and cited the First Amendment. Her lawyer, Preet Bharara, asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to confirm there will be no investigation.
The DOJ has not confirmed a probe, but a spokesperson said public service "should not be met with threats of retribution" and that the department is committed to ending weaponization of government.

Why it matters: Slotkin's own words about deterring young conservatives from public service are now the center of the story, undercutting Democrats' complaints about weaponization as they prepare their own investigations.
